generatedProse.concept-context: Across the School of Sport, marking criteria make the standard explicit, whether for a lab report, a coaching session plan or a management proposal. In sport coaching and physical education they usually judge your knowledge of the subject and principles, the clarity and organisation of the plan or delivery, and your critical reasoning about why you chose each activity rather than mere description. Reading your own work against those dimensions, before you submit or deliver, is how sport students stop guessing what strong work looks like.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students apply the same marking criteria to their own session plan before it is assessed.

Tom reads the plan through, feels it is fine, and submits. Asked which band it meets on coaching rationale, Tom cannot say: the plan lists good drills but does not explain why each one suits the players' stage of development. Tom judged the work by effort and how full the plan looked, not against the criteria, and so missed that it sat a band lower than hoped.

Amara reads the plan against each dimension in turn. Knowledge of coaching principles: strong. Organisation: clear, though the session's progression is rushed. Coaching rationale: thin, mostly a list of activities with little reason given. Amara can name the band each dimension meets and why, and adds the missing rationale before submitting. The judgement is reasoned and tied to the criteria.

Both had the same criteria. Only Amara applied them, and turned the appraisal into a better plan.
generatedProse.summary: Marking criteria in the School of Sport set out the standard your work is judged against, by dimension and level, whether that work is a report, a session plan or a proposal. Applying them to your own draft is self-assessment: you read as an assessor would, name the band each dimension meets, and revise where it falls short. You can now appraise a piece of work against criteria and justify the judgement. The next lesson does the same for the feedback you receive.

check.body: In the worked example, what let Amara justify the grade her session plan would earn?

items.text: She appraised the plan against each dimension of the criteria and could say which band it met and why.
She wrote a longer plan than Tom did.
She submitted the plan earlier than Tom did.
She preferred her own plan to Tom's.

feedback.correct: That's right. Judging each dimension against the criteria is what makes the judgement justifiable.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for how Amara tied the judgement to the criteria.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara could justify the grade because she appraised the plan against each dimension and named the band it met. Length, timing or preference do not justify a judgement.
